passage:
Nine-year-old Charu shuffled into her new class with her shoulders folded forward and her eyes on the floor. At games period the teacher, Naveen, said, "Everybody be a giraffe!" Charu stretched her arms up before she had decided to, and by the third round she was laughing, standing taller than she had all week.

At twenty, Charu spent hour after hour at her library desk before exams. Her neck burned, her back ached and she snapped at her roommate over a borrowed pen. Yusuf, a friend from the next floor, tapped the table. "Ten minutes outside. Bring your notes if you must." They walked round the hostel, and the knot between her shoulder blades loosened.

At twenty-five, Charu got headaches by four o'clock every afternoon and put them down to deadlines. Then she raised her monitor, set a reminder to stand up each hour and walked to the water cooler between calls. Her thoughts felt less sticky by the end of the week, and the deadlines had not changed at all.

qa.q: What did the teacher, Naveen, ask the class to be at games period?
qa.a: Naveen asked everybody to be a giraffe.

qa.q: How do Charu's posture and mood connect at nine, twenty and twenty-five?
qa.a: At nine a hunched, shy body lifts when she stretches up and laughs; at twenty long hours at the desk bring aching neck and back and a short temper; at twenty-five a stiff desk day brings headaches and slow thoughts, and in each case small movement eases both body and mood.

qa.q: What was Charu probably feeling when she snapped at her roommate over the pen?
qa.a: Charu was tired, tense and irritable, with her neck burning and her back aching after hour after hour of study.

qa.q: What small change did Charu make at twenty-five that helped?
qa.a: She raised her monitor, set a reminder to stand each hour and walked to the water cooler, which eased her headaches without changing the deadlines.

grounding: The link between posture and mood across three ages, where body position affects feelings and small movement breaks lift energy.
